data.title: Kinematic Acceleration Explorer
data.description: Analyze how manipulating the applied force versus the inertial mass non-linearly impacts the resulting acceleration through inverse and direct proportionality.
data.context: Newton's Second Law of Motion establishes the foundational proportionality between applied net force, inertial mass, and the resulting linear acceleration of a macroscopic system.

parameters.name: Net Force
parameters.description: The net vector sum of all external forces acting upon the rigid body.

parameters.name: Inertial Mass
parameters.description: The quantitative measure of the body's inertia and resistance to acceleration.

observations.trigger: Increment the Net Force (F) from 50 N to 250 N while keeping the Inertial Mass (m) constant at 10 kg.
observations.prompt: Observe the direct linear proportionality between applied net force and the resulting acceleration vector. How does quintuple magnitude scaling of the numerator impact the temporal rate of velocity change?

observations.trigger: Scale the Inertial Mass (m) from 10 kg to 50 kg while holding the Net Force (F) locked at 100 N.
observations.prompt: Examine the inverse relationship governed by inertial resistance within Newton's Second Law. As mass increases fivefold, what asymptotic behavior do you observe in the system's acceleration curve?

challenges.instruction: Analyze Newton's Second Law. Predict how the resulting linear acceleration of the macroscopic system will respond if the Net Force (F) is increased from its default value of 50 N to a new value of 150 N, assuming the inertial mass remains constant.

Examine the mathematical relationship governing system dynamics. Determine whether the acceleration will increase, decrease, or stay the same if the Inertial Mass (m) is increased from its default value of 10 kg to 40 kg, while the net force remains unchanged.

Consider a scenario where the system's resisting inertia is significantly reduced. Predict the directional change in acceleration if the Inertial Mass (m) is decreased from its default value of 10 kg down to 2 kg, holding the net force constant.
